title: Wesley's warmed heart
hookLine: faith as a living trust you can feel, leading to holy love

cards: "In the evening I went very unwillingly to a society in Aldersgate Street." That's how John Wesley, whom you met in year three, begins the story in his journal. He's an Anglican priest.
He has prayed, fasted, preached and served the poor, and still he doubts he has the faith he preaches. At the meeting, someone is reading aloud from Luther's preface to Paul's letter to the Romans.
And Wesley writes what happened next: "I felt my heart strangely warmed."

teach.b: The journal goes on: "I felt I did trust in Christ, Christ alone, for salvation." Notice what's new. Wesley already knew and preached the faith.
What came that evening was trust he could feel, an assurance in the heart. For Wesley, faith isn't only agreeing that certain statements are true. It's a living trust in God that the heart can know.
But the warmed heart was a beginning, not an ending.
Wesley went on to preach in fields and town squares, to gather people into small groups that prayed together and kept one another honest, and to teach what he called holiness.
And holiness, for Wesley, meant love: loving God with all your heart, and your neighbor as yourself, the commands Jesus calls the first and the second.

Wesley hoped that by God's grace that love could grow until it filled a whole life. Other Christians questioned how far he pressed that hope. Methodist and other Wesleyan churches carry his teaching on.
The Bible has its own warmed hearts.
Two disciples walk to Emmaus with a stranger who turns out to be the risen Jesus, and afterward they say to each other: "Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way?"

And the letter to the Hebrews says: "Follow peace with all men, and holiness, without which no man shall see the Lord." Wesley held those two together. The heart is warmed, and then the warmth goes to work.
A feeling that never reached a neighbor, for him, would have missed the point.

how: Methodist and other Wesleyan Christians remember Wesley's Aldersgate experience, meet in small groups for prayer and accountability, and teach growth in holy love; across churches, Christians speak of faith as heartfelt trust shown in love of neighbor.

games.q: you're Wesley, the morning after your heart was strangely warmed. what comes next?
o: keep the feeling private and wait for it to come again.
go to work: preach, gather people in small groups, and grow in love.
stop praying, since the feeling is what matters.
games.why: for Wesley the warm heart was a beginning. he preached, gathered small groups, and taught holiness as love of God and neighbor.

practice: Put a hand on your chest if you like, feel it rise and fall, and ask gently what's here: warmth, coldness, tiredness, longing, nothing much.
Wesley went to that meeting unwillingly, so whatever you bring is enough to notice, without fixing or judging it. If you pray, you can offer what you find to God, without dressing it up.

wordCard.voice: Wesley's warmed heart. Faith as a living trust you can feel, which, for Wesley, grows into holy love of God and neighbor.
